title: Name the rows a rounded plan breaks

blocks.text: A water utility rounds the LP relaxation of its main-replacement model and wants to know, before anyone reads the rounded plan, which of the model's rows it breaks. Each candidate is a `Project` with a cost and a value ($k), a `must_do` flag, an optional `parent` (the project it depends on) and an optional `group` (a set of alternatives, at most one of which may be funded).

Write `broken_rows(plan, projects, budget)` in `rows.py`. `plan` is the set of funded project ids. With $`P`$ the projects, $`M`$ the must-do ones, $`C`$ the ones with a parent $`p(c)`$, and $`\mathcal{G}`$ the groups, the rows are:

where $`x_i`$ is 1 if $`i`$ is in `plan` and 0 otherwise. Return the set of labels of the rows the plan breaks: `"budget"`, `"must_<pid>"`, `"parent_<pid>"` (the child's id) and `"alt_<group>"`. An allowed plan returns an empty set.
About a dozen lines: one check per row, in the model's order.

"""Run executes this file. Change the calls and see what prints. Submit grades."""
import logging

# Turn the logger up, so the `log.debug` lines of your code show under the printed lines.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

from rows import Project, broken_rows

# Five mains renewals at budget 90.
renewals = [
    Project("R1", 35, 50, must_do=True),
    Project("R2", 25, 30),
    Project("R3", 20, 28, parent="R2"),
    Project("R4", 15, 22, group="pump"),
    Project("R5", 10, 14, group="pump"),
]
for plan in ({"R1", "R2", "R3"}, {"R1", "R3", "R4", "R5"}, {"R2", "R3", "R4"}, {"R1", "R2", "R3", "R4"}):
    print(f"plan {sorted(plan)}:", sorted(broken_rows(plan, renewals, 90)))

    return set()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mains = [Project("M1", 40, 55, must_do=True), Project("M2", 30, 42), Project("M3", 30, 36, parent="M2"),
             Project("M4", 20, 26, group="G1"), Project("M5", 15, 24, group="G1")]
    print(broken_rows({"M1", "M2", "M3", "M4", "M5"}, mains, 100))
    print(broken_rows({"M2", "M3"}, mains, 100))

cases.says: a plan that breaks the budget, a must-do, a parent or an alternative row gets that row's label
spending exactly the budget breaks nothing, since the row is at most
the parent row is one-way: a parent alone is fine, a child alone is not
an alternative group allows one funded project and refuses two

origin.section: Rounding Up, or to the Nearest Whole, Can Break the Budget

concepts: a rounded plan is checked row by row, and each broken row is named by its label
the parent row is one-way and an alternative group allows one funded project
